See the demonstrated corrections in [COPY-CORRECTIONS](../wiki/COPY-CORRECTIONS.md).\\r\\n\\r\\n## Metaphor gives the reader a usable handle\\r\\n\\r\\nThe source uses doors, families, activation, burdens, brackets, and putting yourself in a condition\'s shoes. Each metaphor gives an abstract operation a physical or social handle. A small set of terms recurs, so the reader can keep using it.\\r\\n\\r\\nTransfer the method of choosing a metaphor, not the particular inventory. Prefer a familiar image that helps answer a logical question. Explain its literal meaning immediately. Remove it when it adds more things to remember than it clarifies.\\r\\n\\r\\nFor instance, a ticket can illustrate a requirement only if the rule is stated carefully. “A ticket is required to enter” does not say a ticket guarantees entry. An analogy fails if it smuggles in that reverse.\\r\\n\\r\\nDo not build a competing metaphor for every sentence. Do not invent branded names for every skill. The standard technical terms remain the stable vocabulary.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Humor reduces tension without changing the rule\\r\\n\\r\\nThe source\'s coffee obsession makes an unusual absolute rule memorable. Its reluctant-student aside acknowledges the experience of being asked to guess. The imagined green checkmark gives the reader\'s desire for certainty a recognizable shape.\\r\\n\\r\\nHumor can occur inside an explanation when it makes the thought easier to understand. Joshua\'s source selection supersedes the earlier blanket restriction that wit must stay outside the explanation. It does not authorize mockery, forced slang, exaggerated praise, or an expanding comic story.\\r\\n\\r\\nUse a light aside only when it helps the reader inhabit a situation or relax around a specific mistake. Keep it optional. A paragraph should still teach clearly if the aside is removed. Do not use the source\'s distinctive jokes as templates to be copied.\\r\\n\\r\\nNever turn first-person source anecdotes into Joshua\'s biography. “I ask every student this” requires that Joshua actually does. “Students always learn better this way” requires evidence or a narrower, truthful statement.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Emphasis and visuals identify the decision\\r\\n\\r\\nBold in the source often marks the rule, an inference, a warning, or an instruction. Italics distinguish examples and sometimes emphasize a word that changes the contrast. A table lets the reader compare controlled variations. A STOP asks the reader to attempt something. Do not bold most of a paragraph.\\r\\n- Give an example its own space. Student pages show the assigned work and the lesson itself; internal stage planning, assigned-start metadata, production notes, and selectable difficulty controls do not belong in the teaching prose.\\r\\n\\r\\n## The complete source progression and depth\\r\\n\\r\\nThis map records what the supplied excerpt does in order. It is not an assertion that every future lesson should cover every listed topic.\\r\\n\\r\\n### 1. The relationship comes before its parts\\r\\n\\r\\n**The Art of the If/Then**, HTML lines 142 to 154, opens with a plain definition, a single familiar rule, a literal interpretation, several statements of certainty, and a reason to understand the relationship beneath varied language. The transition promises to take the same example apart.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe depth comes from making “must” meaningful before presenting a list of words. The reader learns what kind of relationship they are looking for. The source also connects certainty to prior “Power Players” material, which is not included in this attachment. Our standalone introduction must supply any needed context itself.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Transfer:** first explain what a conditional says and why its direction matters. Then give a concrete example. Do not open with a diagramming task or make the definition a label attached after a quiz.\\r\\n\\r\\n### 2. Sufficient is explained through presence and absence\\r\\n\\r\\n**The Sufficient Condition**, lines 156 to 199, contains a definition, the recurring anchor, a metaphor, the possibility that the sufficient condition does not occur, a contrast between its absence and presence, and a clarification of “activation.” It then shows **eight indicator rows with eleven displayed example forms**, all expressing the same anchor relationship, and explains why language recognition cannot replace understanding.\\r\\n\\r\\nThis is more than “sufficient goes left.” The text develops what the condition does, what it does not establish, and how wording changes around it.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Transfer:** give sufficient its own explanation, contrasting cases, and nearby practice. A left-side label is useful only after “enough for what?” has a clear answer.\\r\\n\\r\\n### 3. Necessary is developed as a requirement\\r\\n\\r\\n**The Necessary Condition**, lines 201 to 230, defines the other part, reuses the same rule, explains the requirement, and shows **ten indicator rows with eleven displayed forms**. It compares the varied wording with the sufficient-family statements and gives special attention to “only if.” It ends by explaining why symbols help isolate the relationship.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe source uses the ordinary force of “necessary,” “required,” and “need” to make the technical term familiar. Targets can precede the indicator, and familiar words can serve other roles in context. |\\r\\n| Shorten conditions to one or two letters, never more than four. | Joshua\'s clear condensed labels govern. Keep negation, scope, qualifiers, and readability. A short label that loses meaning is not an improvement. |\\r\\n| Try a personalized sufficient guess. | Compare with the whole ordinary meaning and look for a counterexample. It is not a universal instruction to place the next word on the right. |\\r\\n| Confidence guarantees the diagram is correct. | Confidence can grow from practice, but correctness rests on preserving meaning and valid reasoning. Novelty must not obscure the condition or require untaught knowledge. |\\r\\n\\r\\nFor the parcel example, three possible cases distinguish the permitted relationship from an invalid reverse:\\r\\n\\r\\n- Blue sticker and inspected: fits the rule.\\r\\n- Inspected without a blue sticker: also fits the rule.\\r\\n- Blue sticker without inspection: breaks the rule.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe rule does not itself say any such parcel exists. Examples of possible cases illustrate consistency, not existence claims. This distinction matters when moving from individual facts to general rules.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Calibration examples for different LSAT surfaces\\r\\n\\r\\nAll examples below are original drafts for this reference. They demonstrate writing mechanisms; they are not assigned work or approved curriculum.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Explain sufficient and necessary without rushing\\r\\n\\r\\n> Every parcel with a blue sticker has been inspected.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Suppose yours has a blue sticker. That\'s enough to know it has been inspected. You don\'t need another fact about the parcel. The rule has already told you what must be true of every parcel with that sticker.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> We call the blue sticker the **sufficient condition**. Sufficient means enough. Here, enough to establish inspection under this rule.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Inspection is the **necessary condition**. A blue-sticker parcel has to meet that requirement. Otherwise it would be an exception to a rule that allows no exceptions.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Now suppose a parcel has been inspected. Does it have to have a blue sticker?\\r\\n>\\r\\n> We still don\'t know. Inspection was required for the blue-sticker parcels. The shop never said those were the only parcels it inspected.\\r\\n\\r\\nThis returns to meaning at every term. The example does not assert why the shop uses stickers or when they are applied. Those extra facts are unnecessary.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Teach a necessary expression through its whole meaning\\r\\n\\r\\n> Editing this newsletter requires an account.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> What does the sentence say the editor needs? An account. Keep that complete idea on the required side of the relationship:\\r\\n>\\r\\n> **Edits this newsletter → Has an account**\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Read it back: if someone edits this newsletter, they have an account. That matches the sentence.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Try the reverse. If someone has an account, do they necessarily edit the newsletter? The sentence hasn\'t told us that. An account could belong to someone who only reads it.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe final possible counterexample is introduced as something consistent with the sentence, not an asserted fact about this system. Technical placement has a semantic reason.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Give a flashcard a reasoning task\\r\\n\\r\\n**Front**\\r\\n\\r\\n> Every package in Locker 4 has been scanned. A package has been scanned. Must it be in Locker 4? Why?\\r\\n\\r\\n**Back**\\r\\n\\r\\n> No. The rule tells us about packages already in Locker 4. It doesn\'t say every scanned package goes there.\\r\\n\\r\\nThis is more useful than a card that only asks “Necessary condition = which side?” Keep simple recall cards when recall is the actual skill; do not mistake that for complete reasoning practice.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Make feedback identify the missed connection\\r\\n\\r\\n> You used the sentence in the reverse direction. “Only registered visitors enter the archive” requires registration for entry. It hasn\'t said every registered visitor enters. Read the diagram as **Enters → Registered** and compare it with the sentence.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe feedback names the mistake, shows the relevant meaning, and gives a repair. It avoids generic praise, mockery, and labels such as “weak reasoning.”\\r\\n\\r\\n### Explain an ordinary learning objection\\r\\n\\r\\n> “I understood the sentence. Why write it down?”\\r\\n>\\r\\n> With one short rule, you may not need to. When a passage gives you several relationships, a diagram lets you compare them without rereading the wording each time. In this exercise, write the relationship so we can check that you kept its direction and complete ideas.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe answer gives a decision criterion and distinguishes the purpose of this exercise from a blanket rule about every test question.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Transfer the voice to another LSAT topic\\r\\n\\r\\n> A conclusion is the claim the author is asking you to accept. The other statements are supposed to support it.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Nora says, “The library should stay open later because every evening seat was taken this week.” What is she trying to persuade us of?\\r\\n>\\r\\n> That the library should stay open later. The full seats are her reason. She expects that reason to support the proposed change.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> You don\'t have to agree with her. First, separate what she wants you to accept from what she gives you in support.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe same mechanism works outside conditionals: definition, small example, question, explanation, and a useful boundary. No conditional topic has been imported into the conclusion lesson.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Revise the draft in a useful order\\r\\n\\r\\n### First, check the reasoning and scope\\r\\n\\r\\nList what is given, what follows, and why. Try to construct a case that satisfies the given information but makes the proposed conclusion false. If that case is possible, revise the logic before polishing the voice. Check modality, negation, quantifier scope, and whether the learner has actually been taught every required operation.\\r\\n\\r\\nFor a rewrite, preserve Joshua\'s established method and explicit lesson scope. The new reference governs delivery. It does not authorize removing content that students need or adding source topics the current assignment does not cover.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Then, check the learner\'s experience\\r\\n\\r\\nRead as someone who has never seen the notation. Can they tell what the concept is? Can they answer the first question with what the page has taught? Does each new term refer to an idea they have seen? Does the page tell them why the correct answer follows?\\r\\n\\r\\nPut the explanation beside the point where it is needed. Do not rely on an interaction to imply a distinction the prose never explains. A student who cannot use the animation must still be able to learn from the text.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Then, listen to the voice\\r\\n\\r\\nRead aloud at an ordinary teaching pace. Replace stiff phrasing with the words the teacher would naturally use. Keep the intermediate thoughts. Vary sentence length where the task changes. Repair the missing reasoning, the abrupt transition, or the abstract example.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Finally, verify the student surface\\r\\n\\r\\nCheck the actual prompt, answer state, labels, buttons, diagrams, and explanations. A good note can be undermined by a shell that exposes internal planning or reveals the answer too soon. Preview desktop and mobile when the interface changes. Keep the instructor\'s planning map separate from what the learner sees.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Use this rubric before handing over LSAT writing\\r\\n\\r\\nScore each dimension from 0 to 2: **0** absent or misleading; **1** partly present but needing revision; **2** clear and usable. This is an editorial tool, not a validated learning measure. A logical error or scope violation requires revision regardless of the total.\\r\\n\\r\\n| Dimension | What a strong draft does |\\r\\n|---|---|\\r\\n| **Ordinary meaning** | Defines the idea in language the reader can understand before notation. |\\r\\n| **Concrete anchor** | Uses an original, small, unambiguous situation and states needed assumptions. |\\r\\n| **Visible reasoning** | Shows the intermediate connection instead of asserting a result. |\\r\\n| **Point of view** | Keeps the reader involved; uses teacher narration purposefully. |\\r\\n| **Cadence** | Gives complex thoughts room and short conclusions a clear place to land. |\\r\\n| **Vocabulary** | Keeps useful technical terms, explains them, and avoids internal jargon. |\\r\\n| **Questions and pauses** | Asks a genuine decision and gives an appropriate chance to answer. |\\r\\n| **Boundaries** | Shows what the information leaves open and why a tempting move fails. |\\r\\n| **Progression** | Each operation has a prerequisite, a reason to appear, and adequate practice. |\\r\\n| **Transfer** | Fresh questions require the taught skill, with reasoned feedback. |\\r\\n| **Tone and warmth** | Expects effort, supports the next action, and never mocks uncertainty. |\\r\\n| **Presentation** | Examples, comparisons, notation, and interactions clarify the reasoning. |\\r\\n\\r\\nDo not treat a high total as proof of an identical voice. Use the original source and Joshua\'s response to calibrate the subjective feel. His concrete corrections override a score.\\r\\n\\r\\n## A reusable writing brief\\r\\n\\r\\nUse this when giving another writer or agent the task. Supply the actual source, lesson scope, prerequisite knowledge, and approved method along with it.\\r\\n\\r\\n```text\\r\\nWrite this LSAT material in Joshua\'s selected teaching voice.\\r\\nRead wiki/teaching-voice.md, references/lsat-teaching-voice-standard.md,\\r\\nand wiki/COPY-CORRECTIONS.md before drafting.\\r\\n\\r\\nKeep the reader beside the teacher. Start with the ordinary meaning of\\r\\nthe idea, then make it concrete with an original, intuitive example.\\r\\nShow each small inference in natural language. Ask the question a learner\\r\\nwould actually need to answer here. When the question is practice, leave\\r\\nroom for an attempt before revealing the reasoning.\\r\\n\\r\\nVary sentence length by purpose. Use contractions naturally.\\r\\nTeach the technical term when there is a clear idea to attach it to.\\r\\nRepeat an anchor only when the repetition changes the learner\'s view.\\r\\nShow a tempting mistake and how to detect it when that distinction matters.\\r\\n\\r\\nPreserve Joshua\'s method, the exact logical strength, complete conditions,\\r\\nand the selected topic scope. This is the canonical voice doc: route all student-facing and brand copy through it. Built from a grill with Joshua (2026-06-13), then tested and enriched against the full corpus of his real correspondence (944 messages he authored, mid-2025 to mid-2026, from the Gmail takeout; 2026-07-18). Claims below marked with a quote are evidenced by that corpus.\\r\\n\\r\\nIt replaces the old two-register / 15-named-tools \\"preserve verbatim\\" profile (deleted 2026-06-10) and folds in the brand/marketing register the earlier draft was missing.\\r\\n\\r\\n**LSAT teaching standard, selected 2026-10-02:** Joshua chose the supplied Conditional Reasoning transcription as the reference for how LSAT material should sound and unfold. Read [LSAT teaching voice standard](../references/lsat-teaching-voice-standard.md) before drafting lessons, notes, explanations, drills, flashcards, quizzes, or instructional feedback. It contains the detailed source analysis, original calibration examples, progression, and review rubric. [Source identity and limits](sources/conditional-reasoning-voice.md) are preserved separately. This choice develops the teaching-content register below; correspondence and marketing retain their own registers.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Core voice (every register)\\r\\n\\r\\nThe constant under all three registers below. This is Joshua on the page.\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Quiet authority.** State the value and let it land. Never oversell, never beg, never perform enthusiasm.\\r\\n- **Specific, never generic.** Real scores, the actual skill, the student\'s own history. Praise is a specific observation, not \\"great job.\\"\\r\\n- **Honest about the work, gentle about the person.** Be blunt that the LSAT is hard (\\"expect this to be exhausting and very challenging\\"). Never be blunt about a student\'s shortcomings. Honesty points at the material; warmth points at the person. When someone slips, nudge gently, never accuse.\\r\\n- **Light, grounded metaphor, understated in email.** In his real correspondence the recurring image is quiet: \\"partner with you on your LSAT journey,\\" \\"getting set up,\\" \\"foundational.\\" The vivid images (runway, climb, march toward November, an easy door to walk through) belong to authored teaching and brand copy, not to email. Keep metaphor light and grounded; never float off into abstraction.\\r\\n- **Balanced rhythm.** Air between ideas. Real correspondence is short and single-purpose (median ~280 characters). In teaching, vary sentence and paragraph length with the reasoning: give an explanation room, then let a short sentence settle the consequence. Do not impose email brevity on a lesson or cut its intermediate reasoning.\\r\\n- **Plain professional diction.** No corporate jargon, no startup hype (\\"unlock,\\" \\"crush,\\" \\"level up,\\" \\"game-changer\\"; \\"crush\\" appears once in 944 messages). Contractions are the norm, not the exception. Exclamation points are genuine, not performed: a warm message often carries one, occasionally more, especially in openers (\\"Sorry for such a long delay!\\"). He is not exclamation-averse.\\r\\n- **Forward-looking.** End on the next step or what\'s ahead.\\r\\n- **No em dashes, ever.** Use periods, colons before lists, the middot (·) as a separator, and numbered steps for procedures.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Openings, closings, and signature phrases\\r\\n\\r\\nThe mechanical fingerprint of his email, from the real corpus. Match these when drafting as Joshua.\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Greeting.** \\"Hi [Name],\\" is the default (used ~519x). \\"Hey [Name],\\" for established/returning students (~229x, warmer). \\"Hello [Name],\\" (~105x) and \\"Dear [Name],\\" (~18x, formal) for first contact or a more formal note.\\r\\n- **Sign-off.** \\"Best,\\" and \\"Best regards,\\" are the workhorses (~360x / ~237x). \\"Thanks,\\" when it\'s a favor or logistics (~146x). \\"Warmly,\\" / \\"Warm regards,\\" (~54x) for a genuinely warm note. \\"Talk soon,\\" (~9x) for someone he\'ll see again soon.\\r\\n- **Signature.** Almost always signed **\\"Joshua\\"** (844 of 944 messages). The name is near-universal; include it.\\r\\n- **Signature phrases (his verbal fingerprint, use naturally, don\'t overuse):** \\"let me know\\" (by far the most common, ~390x), \\"looking forward,\\" \\"I hope\\" / \\"hope all is well\\" / \\"hope you,\\" \\"no worries at all,\\" \\"happy to\\" / \\"more than happy to,\\" \\"just wanted to make sure,\\" \\"make sure,\\" \\"no rush,\\" \\"of course.\\"\\r\\n- **Punctuation he actually uses:** semicolons (correctly, ~41x); ellipses essentially never. (For em-dashes, the hard rule in Core voice governs: never.)\\r\\n\\r\\n## The apology / accountability move\\r\\n\\r\\nOne of his most frequent and characteristic behaviors, and worth naming on its own. When he is late to reply, or missed or mishandled something, he opens by owning it plainly, often with a brief honest reason, then pivots straight to the fix. No over-apologizing, no excuses dressed up.\\r\\n\\r\\n> I\'m so sorry. I thought I had let you know ... I clearly didn\'t communicate that as well as I should have.\\r\\n\\r\\n> I\'ve been away from work for personal reasons, but I\'m back now and getting caught up.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe pattern: own it in the first line, give the real reason in one clause, move to what happens next. Warm, candid, brief.\\r\\n\\r\\n## When something on his side broke (approved shape, 2026-09-11)\\r\\n\\r\\nFrom the Sandra booking-error reply, edited by Joshua line by line over three drafts and then sent as-is. Use this shape whenever a student hit a bug or a mistake that was his. The sent text is the reference:\\r\\n\\r\\n> Hi Sandra,\\r\\n>\\r\\n> I\'m sorry about this. The error was on my end, not yours.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> To confirm: none of your bookings went through, so nothing is on the calendar yet. The page was showing a few times that the system then refused, and it looks like you landed on those. That is fixed now.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Your link is the same one as before:\\r\\n> [link]\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Pick any time it shows and it will book. If it\'s easier, just send me the time you were trying for and I\'ll add it to the schedule myself.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> If you run into any other issues, let me know.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Once again, my apologies.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Best,\\r\\n> Joshua\\r\\n\\r\\n1. **Apology first, as the opening line.** \\"I\'m sorry about this. The error was on my end, not yours.\\" The ownership sits in the first two sentences, before any explanation.\\r\\n2. **State their position plainly, as a confirmation.** \\"To confirm: none of your bookings went through, so nothing is on the calendar yet.\\" Answer the question they actually asked. Don\'t mention the package or credits unless the situation calls for it.\\r\\n3. **One-sentence explanation, then \\"That is fixed now.\\"** No mechanics, no system names.\\r\\n4. **Hand them the next step, plus the manual fallback.** The link, \\"pick any time it shows and it will book,\\" and the offer to do it by hand: \\"If it\'s easier, just send me the time you were trying for and I\'ll add it to the schedule myself.\\"\\r\\n5. **Invite the next report:** \\"If you run into any other issues, let me know.\\"\\r\\n6. **Close with \\"Once again, my apologies.\\"** then \\"Best,\\" and \\"Joshua\\".\\r\\n\\r\\nCut from the draft, do not reuse:\\r\\n- \\"Sorry for the runaround\\" as a sign-off. The apology opens the email; it is not a closing quip.\\r\\n- \\"You will get a calendar invite with the Google Meet link right after.\\" Do not narrate what the system will send; it reads as a promise about machinery.\\r\\n- \\"You have all 10 sessions\\" / \\"nothing was used from your package.\\" Leave the package out unless it is needed; the reassurance they want is that nothing is booked, not an accounting.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Situational micro-templates\\r\\n\\r\\nVerbatim-grounded reference lines for the situations that recur most. Adapt, never paste blindly.\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Student reschedules / cancels:** low-pressure, no guilt.\\r\\n  > No worries at all. It happens, so please don\'t worry about it. If you would like to reschedule, just let me know.\\r\\n- **He missed / no-showed (approved make-good template):** full ownership, real reason, offer to make it right (see the apology move above). When the cause was an unexpected health issue, the approved shape is: sincerely apologize, state that a serious health scare unexpectedly took him out of commission, offer a **completely free, full LSAT session**, and hand them the complimentary booking link `https://cal.com/joshua-jtx5ud/complimentary-session`. Emphasis stays limited: bold the complimentary offer, italicize the line that one focused session can put points on the board. Draft in Gmail; never send without Joshua\'s explicit go-ahead.\\r\\n- **Consultation reminder (day-of):**\\r\\n  > Just checking in before our consultation today. Looking forward to speaking with you. I just wanted to make sure everything is still good.\\r\\n- **Consultation follow-up:** warm, specific to their situation.\\r\\n  > Really nice meeting you. I enjoyed our conversation ... I\'m glad we got to talk through where you\'re at and what you\'re aiming for on test day.\\r\\n- **Inbound prospect (hasn\'t booked):** state availability plainly, no overselling, hand them the next step.\\r\\n  > Thanks for reaching out ... I\'d be happy to talk more about what you\'re working on and see if we\'d be a good fit. You can schedule a consultation here.\\r\\n- **Student under real-life stress:** meet the person first.\\r\\n  > Please don\'t apologize ... it sounds like you are dealing with an incredibly stressful and demanding situation.\\r\\n\\r\\n## The three registers\\r\\n\\r\\nWhich voice governs which surface.\\r\\n\\r\\n### 1. Coaching (earnest) -- inbox, personal encouragement, email\\r\\n\\r\\nFully earnest. Warm, sincere, calm, patient. No jokes. The closest thing to being in the room with Joshua. Normalizes struggle, then moves to the work.\\r\\n\\r\\nReference line (target tone):\\r\\n\\r\\n> Totally normal to trip on this one. Let\'s slow down: what is the author actually concluding? Once you see it, the trap answers lose their grip. You\'ve got this.\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Encouragement (student missed a hard one):** honest first, then forward. Name that it\'s genuinely hard, stay calm, move to the work. Not soft-reassuring, not cold.\\r\\n  > Missing this is expected. It\'s one of the hardest moves on the test. Let\'s slow down and see where it slipped.\\r\\n- **Accountability (student isn\'t doing the work):** gentle nudge, low pressure. Frame it as a slip, find a rhythm together. Never \\"the reps aren\'t happening,\\" never tough love.\\r\\n- **Praise (student nails it):** name the exact skill, tie it to their history, raise the bar.\\r\\n  > That\'s the cleanest you\'ve split premise from conclusion yet. Let\'s push it into the harder sets.\\r\\n- **Hard truth about the test:** state it plainly. \\"Do not expect for it to come easy. Expect to find this exhausting.\\"\\r\\n\\r\\n### 2. Teaching content (conversational reasoning) -- lessons, recaps, notes, drills, explanations\\r\\n\\r\\nUse [LSAT teaching voice standard](../references/lsat-teaching-voice-standard.md), Joshua\'s selected calibration from 2026-10-02. Keep the reader beside the teacher. Explain the ordinary meaning, ground it in an original example, make the small inferences audible, ask a useful question, and show both the consequence and its limit. Introduce terminology and notation when their meaning is established. Give each concept enough development to be learned from the page.\\r\\n\\r\\nContractions and varied sentence lengths should sound natural when read aloud. Repetition should change the reader\'s view of the same relationship. Questions should give the reader actual thinking work. Light humor may appear within an explanation when it helps understanding; this supersedes the older wit-only-at-the-edges restriction. Do not force punchlines, slang, hyperbole, catchphrases, or paragraph quotas.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe source governs delivery, not Joshua\'s procedure, indicator taxonomy, biography, or the scope of a lesson. Preserve his approved methods and logical precision. Personal encouragement still follows the earnest coaching register. Brand (sharp wit) -- landing, auth, marketing\\r\\n\\r\\nConfident and clever, the way a good lawyer is clever. Wit tied to the real skill, not wordplay for its own sake. Playful is allowed, but every clever line must be earned and true. Hollow cleverness fails (the killed \\"the next card is the page in front of you\\" was clever but empty).\\r\\n\\r\\n> Most prep teaches the test. Review the whole note for repeated umbrella instructions and make task instructions executable. This follows the teaching voice: specific, concrete, short sentences, with air between distinct ideas.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Fact and rule definitions must explain the inference (2026-09-30)\\r\\n\\r\\nJoshua rejected definitions that remained abstract and an explanation that did not clearly distinguish applying a rule from linking rules. The Some, Most, and All reference also governs the progression: introduce the whole idea, develop the individual components, then compare and combine them. A visual refresh must review that sequence, not only colors and boxes.\\r\\n\\r\\n### \\"Concept lesson\\" → the actual reasoning title (2026-09-30)\\r\\n\\r\\nThe recap preview exposed an internal label above the student lesson. Application files remain unchanged pending the parent's authorization following Claude plan review. This draft follows the project-owned LSAT U voice skill, the full selected teaching standard, canonical teaching voice, and demonstrated copy corrections.\n+\n+The ready/packed example remains the original anchor. No later topic is introduced as an opening operation.\n+\n+## Orientation: What are conditionals?\n+\n+Hero subtitle: A conditional tells us that if one thing is true, something else has to be true too. Let's see what that connection lets you conclude, and what it leaves open.\n+\n+### One condition tells you something else\n+\n+A condition is something that can be true or false of the situation we're considering. A door is open. A person has a ticket. An order has been packed. Each gives us an idea whose truth we can ask about.\n+\n+A conditional statement connects two conditions. It says that if the first is true, the other has to be true too. It doesn't tell us that the first condition actually occurred. It tells us what would follow if it did.\n+\n+That distinction matters. You can understand a rule about people who have tickets without knowing whether anyone has a ticket. Later, a fact about one person may give you a way to use that rule.\n+\n+Visual: two ordinary-language panels, “If this condition is met...” and “...the other condition has to be true.” No arrow or sufficient/necessary labels yet.\n+\n+### Why learn this?\n+\n+On the LSAT, you're often deciding whether a conclusion follows from what you've been told. A conditional may supply the connection you need. It can also help you see exactly where an argument asks you to accept more than its information supports.\n+\n+The important part is the direction. If one condition guarantees another, can we start with the other condition and go back? Sometimes another statement allows that. But the first rule alone may not.\n+\n+We'll work with one everyday rule and change the fact we know about a particular order. You'll see a conclusion the rule supports and another that would need more information. That's the distinction you'll use when checking what must be true or deciding whether an argument has gone too far.\n+\n+### A guarantee is stronger than a tendency\n+\n+Compare these statements:\n+\n+**Orders marked ready are usually packed.**\n+\n+**Every order marked ready has been packed.**\n+\n+Usually leaves room for exceptions. You could find an order marked ready that hasn't been packed and still accept the first statement. The second statement doesn't leave that possibility open. Every order with that label has been packed.\n+\n+For an LSAT question, take the stated rule as given. A real shop could make a mistake, but we're asking what follows from this particular statement. The conditional gives us a guarantee within the information we're considering.\n+\n+### Read one rule in ordinary English\n+\n+**Every order marked ready has been packed.**\n+\n+There are two complete ideas here: an order is marked ready, and an order has been packed. The sentence tells us something about every order that meets the first condition.\n+\n+Read it this way: if an order is marked ready, then it has been packed. We don't need to know why the shop uses that label. We need to know what the sentence tells us about an order that has it.\n+\n+Prediction pause: **Order A is marked ready. What do we now know about it?**\n+\n+Reveal: **Order A has been packed.** The rule covers every order marked ready, and the fact tells us that Order A is one of those orders. That's the connection. The rule tells us what has to be true of the group; the fact lets us apply it to this case.\n+\n+We haven't learned that every order in the shop is packed. Our conclusion concerns Order A because that's the order the fact tells us about.\n+\n+### The arrow is a shorter way to write it\n+\n+Now that we understand the sentence, we can give the two conditions shorter labels. The arrow records the connection between them:\n+\n+**Marked ready → Packed**\n+\n+Read it from left to right: if the order is marked ready, then it has been packed. The left condition gives us enough information to establish the right condition under this rule.\n+\n+The arrow doesn't mean “and then.” Packing could happen before the label is added. It also doesn't claim that the label causes the packing. We're recording what follows logically, so the same diagram can preserve a relationship whose real-world events happen in a different order.\n+\n+### Change the fact, keep the rule\n+\n+Keep the rule exactly the same. This time, the fact tells us about packing:\n+\n+**Every order marked ready has been packed.**\n+\n+Prediction pause: **Order B has been packed. Do we know whether it is marked ready?**\n+\n+Reveal: **We don't know yet.** Order B could be marked ready. It could also be packed and waiting for a ready label. Both possibilities fit the statement.\n+\n+The rule tells us about every ready order. It hasn't told us that every packed order gets that label. To conclude that Order B is ready, we'd need that additional connection.\n+\n+Existing SetExplorer follows. Explain the picture first: the ready orders sit inside the packed orders because every ready order is packed. A packed order can fit inside or outside the ready group. The picture shows allowed arrangements; the rule doesn't require the two groups to have different sizes.\n+\n+### Try the same reasoning with a new rule\n+\n+You've used the rule in its stated direction and checked what happens when you start from its result. Try that distinction with a different sentence.\n+\n+Keep the existing fresh badge check and its option-specific feedback. Add a sentence after it: A matching result can make the reverse feel plausible. Check whether the sentence actually gave you that direction before accepting it.\n+\n+End transition: We can now name the two different jobs the conditions are doing. One is enough to establish the other. The other is required whenever the first holds.\n+\n+## Sufficient and necessary: What is enough, and what is required?\n+\n+Hero subtitle: The same rule gives its two conditions different jobs. Let's take each one seriously before giving it a place in the diagram.\n+\n+### Sufficient means enough\n+\n+Return to our order:\n+\n+**Every order marked ready has been packed.**\n+\n+If you know an order is marked ready, you have enough information to conclude it has been packed. You don't need a second fact about its contents. The rule already tells you what must be true of every order with that label.\n+\n+We call being marked ready the sufficient condition. Sufficient means enough. Here, enough to establish that the order has been packed under this particular rule.\n+\n+Prediction pause: **Order C is marked ready. Do you need another fact about C to know it has been packed?**\n+\n+Reveal: No. The ready label meets the condition the rule tells us about. The rule and that fact are enough to establish packing. This doesn't make the label the only possible way to find out that an order is packed.\n+\n+Existing GateExplorer follows the reveal. Keep meaningful labels and readable roles.\n+\n+### Enough does not mean the only way\n+\n+Suppose Order D isn't marked ready. We no longer have the fact that allowed us to use the rule in its stated direction. But that doesn't settle the packing question.\n+\n+Prediction pause: **Order D isn't marked ready. Could it still have been packed?**\n+\n+Reveal: Yes. D could be packed and waiting for its label. It could also be unpacked. Neither possibility creates a ready order that hasn't been packed, so both fit the rule.\n+\n+This is why “enough” needs care. The sentence gives us one condition that settles packing. It hasn't said packing happens only for those orders. When that sufficient condition isn't present, the other condition may still be true.\n+\n+Keep the existing collected/receipt check. Its fresh rule checks whether the learner recognizes the sufficient role in a new situation.\n+\n+### Necessary means required\n+\n+Now look at the other condition in the same rule. An order marked ready has to have been packed. Packing is required for an order to meet the ready condition without breaking the rule.\n+\n+We call being packed the necessary condition. Necessary means required. It names something that has to be true whenever the sufficient condition is true.\n+\n+Ask “required for what?” Here, required for an order marked ready under this rule. The relationship gives the word its meaning. Being packed isn't permanently a necessary condition in every sentence about orders.\n+\n+Prediction pause: **Which condition does a ready order have to meet under this rule?**\n+\n+Reveal: It has to be packed. Otherwise we'd have a ready order that wasn't packed, which the sentence rules out. The ready label is enough to establish packing, and packing is required for every ready order. Those are two views of the same relationship.\n+\n+Then show the existing two-role visual, with “Enough to establish packing” beside ready and “Required for every ready order” beside packed.\n+\n+### Having a requirement does not guarantee the result\n+\n+Let's use a different requirement:\n+\n+**Entering the archive requires a pass.**\n+\n+The sentence tells us what someone needs for entry: a pass. If someone enters the archive, they have that pass. That's why “has a pass” belongs on the required side.\n+\n+**Enters the archive → Has a pass**\n+\n+Prediction pause: **Mina has a pass. Does this sentence establish that she entered the archive?**\n+\n+Reveal: No. Mina could have a pass and remain outside. The rule tells us what entry requires; it doesn't tell us that every person with a pass enters. To make that conclusion, we'd need a rule giving the pass that additional job.\n+\n+Necessary doesn't mean enough. A requirement can be present while the other condition remains unknown. Keep the existing finalist/invitation check to test the distinction with a new rule.\n+\n+### Read the roles in the relationship\n+\n+When you see **Marked ready → Packed**, the left condition is sufficient for the right: it's enough to establish it. The right condition is necessary for the left: it's required whenever the left holds.\n+\n+The names describe roles in this rule. A different sentence could give the same idea a different role. So don't ask whether “a pass” is sufficient or necessary by itself. Ask what the complete sentence says having the pass does.\n+\n+The next two groups give us ways to recognize these roles in varied wording. We'll keep returning to the meaning because a familiar word can only help if you know what complete idea it refers to.\n+\n+## Group 1: Find what is enough\n+\n+Hero subtitle: These expressions can point to the sufficient idea. Read what each one says before deciding which complete condition belongs on the left.\n+\n+Opening explanation: You already know what a sufficient condition does. When it holds, the rule gives you the other condition. Group 1 helps you recognize that job in several kinds of sentence. We'll work through the meaning of each expression, then practice finding its complete target.\n+\n+### If: the starting condition can come last\n+\n+**A report is reviewed if it is submitted before noon.**\n+\n+Read the if-clause first: the report is submitted before noon. The sentence makes that enough for review. A report meeting that condition has to be reviewed under this rule.\n+\n+The target of if is the complete idea “submitted before noon.” It appears second in the sentence, but it still has the sufficient role. The order of the clauses doesn't change what guarantees what.\n+\n+Prediction pause: **Which fact lets you use this rule to establish review: submission before noon, or review itself?**\n+\n+Reveal: Submission before noon. Write **Submitted before noon → Reviewed**. Read it in ordinary English and compare it with the original. Starting from review instead would make a new promise about submission time that this sentence hasn't given us.\n+\n+### When: an occasion can supply enough information\n+\n+**When the alarm sounds, the staff evacuate.**\n+\n+In this stated rule, the alarm sounding is enough for the staff to evacuate. When refers to that complete event. We're treating the sentence as an exceptionless relationship, rather than making a prediction about what staff usually do.\n+\n+Prediction pause: **The staff are evacuating. Does this rule establish that the alarm sounded?**\n+\n+Reveal: No. It tells us what follows when the alarm sounds. It hasn't said an alarm is the only possible reason for evacuation. Write **Alarm sounds → Staff evacuate**. “The staff evacuate when the alarm sounds” expresses the same direction even though the event comes last.\n+\n+### Where: keep the location attached\n+\n+**Where a station is available, the service operates.**\n+\n+The sentence tells us about a location where a station is available. At that location, station availability is enough for the service to operate. Where refers to the station being available, not to service in some unrelated place.\n+\n+Prediction pause: **A station is available at North Square. What does the sentence establish about North Square?**\n+\n+Reveal: The service operates there. Write **Station available at a location → Service operates there**. Keep the location the same on both sides. The statement hasn't given us a conclusion about another square whose station status we don't know.\n+\n+### All: name the complete group\n+\n+**All registered guests receive a wristband.**\n+\n+The statement covers each registered guest. Once you know someone is a registered guest, you can conclude that person receives a wristband. Registered matters: the rule doesn't tell us about every guest regardless of registration.\n+\n+Prediction pause: **Nora is a guest, but we haven't been told whether she's registered. Does the rule settle her wristband status?**\n+\n+Reveal: No. The fact doesn't yet put Nora in the complete group the rule covers. Write **Registered guest → Receives wristband**. Keep the modifier when you shorten the condition; leaving out registered changes the rule.\n+\n+### The only: read the whole expression\n+\n+**The only vehicles permitted inside are electric vehicles.**\n+\n+The sentence limits the vehicles permitted inside. Every vehicle in that group has to be electric. Start by asking “the only what?” The target is vehicles permitted inside, not electric vehicles.\n+\n+Prediction pause: **You learn a vehicle was permitted inside. What does the sentence tell you about it?**\n+\n+Reveal: It is electric. Write **Vehicle permitted inside → Electric vehicle**. The sentence hasn't promised that every electric vehicle is admitted. An electric vehicle that remains outside would fit the rule.\n+\n+This is why the only belongs with our sufficient expressions: the complete group it introduces gives us the starting condition. We'll compare it with only in Group 2. Read the complete expression now so that the missing or added word doesn't quietly change your interpretation.\n+\n+### Every: each qualifying case gets the result\n+\n+**Every finalist receives an invitation.**\n+\n+This gives finalist status the same sufficient job that all gave registered-guest status. Choose any person who is a finalist and the statement settles the invitation question for that person.\n+\n+Prediction pause: **Someone receives an invitation. Have we established that they are a finalist?**\n+\n+Reveal: No. Every finalist receives one, but the sentence hasn't restricted invitations to finalists. Write **Finalist → Receives invitation**. The direction comes from which people the statement covers, not from which condition appears most important.\n+\n+### Any: keep the restriction with the person\n+\n+**Any applicant who submits late pays a fee.**\n+\n+Any covers each applicant who meets the stated restriction. That whole idea is enough for the fee: the person is an applicant and submits late. Applicant alone doesn't capture it.\n+\n+Prediction pause: **Which label preserves the sufficient condition: “Applicant” or “Applicant submits late”?**\n+\n+Reveal: Applicant submits late. Write **Applicant submits late → Pays fee**. “A fee is paid by any applicant who submits late” moves the target later without changing it. Locate what any refers to rather than treating sentence position as a placement instruction.\n+\n+### Find the target, then place it\n+\n+Now use the existing TranslationLab. Keep its two-stage decision: identify the complete target, then place it left. Explain: “Add what to the indicator when that gives you a sensible question. If what? All what? The only what? Your answer should be the whole idea the expression refers to. Then check whether that idea really is enough to establish the other condition.”\n+\n+Keep the existing limiting-modifier check, the only comparison, fresh DiagramBuilder, seven fresh recall sentences, and final meaning check. Strengthen the practical diagram instruction: “If you know the meaning but hesitate over the arrow, imagine the left condition is true. Does the sentence then require the right condition? Read the whole relationship in English. If it makes a promise the original didn't make, change the direction.”\n+\n+## Group 2: Find what is required\n+\n+Hero subtitle: These expressions can identify a requirement. Find the complete idea the sentence says you need, then check what its presence does and does not prove.\n+\n+Opening explanation: Group 1 helped us find a condition that is enough. Group 2 turns our attention to what must be true when the other condition holds. A requirement belongs on the right because the left condition cannot hold under the rule without it. Having the requirement, though, may leave the left condition unknown.\n+\n+### Only: find the people the result is limited to\n+\n+**Only members are admitted.**\n+\n+Admission is limited to members. So if someone is admitted, the sentence tells us they're a member. Only refers to members, and membership has the necessary role.\n+\n+Prediction pause: **Leon is a member. Does this sentence promise that Leon is admitted?**\n+\n+Reveal: No. Membership is required, but a member could remain outside. Write **Admitted → Member**. This preserves the restriction on admission without adding a promise about every member.\n+\n+Compare “The only people admitted are members.” That sentence also tells us every admitted person is a member. Its expression points to a different target, admitted people, while the full relationship remains the same. The only gives us the sufficient target; only gives us the necessary target. Read the whole sentence in both cases.\n+\n+### Only if: a condition that must be met\n+\n+**A student graduates only if the student completes the project.**\n+\n+The student needs to complete the project for graduation. The sentence makes project completion a requirement; it hasn't made it a promise of graduation.\n+\n+Prediction pause: **A student completed the project. Could the student still fail to graduate without contradicting this sentence?**\n+\n+Reveal: Yes. The sentence hasn't told us that completion is the only requirement or that every student who completes the project graduates. Write **Graduates → Completes project**. The target of only if is the complete condition “completes the project,” which goes right.\n+\n+Keep DirectionSwitch here. Introduce it with the meaning: “Watch what changes when only is added to if. Filing a complaint is necessary for a review to occur under the stated rule. It isn't stated enough to produce a review.\n+\n+Prediction pause: **A complaint has been filed. A filed complaint with no review fits this statement. “Only when a complaint is filed does a review occur” moves the required condition to the front, but it keeps the same relationship.\n+\n+### Only where: keep the requirement at the same place\n+\n+**The service operates only where a station is available.**\n+\n+The service needs a station wherever it operates. Only where points to station availability as the requirement. The requirement appears before required, but its role hasn't changed. Read the whole sentence to locate what is required. Automatically taking the words after the indicator would point you toward entry and reverse the rule.\n+\n+The current pass still doesn't guarantee entry.       paragraphs: [

        "The statement doesn't tell us who the finalists are. It tells us what has to be true of each one. A separate fact about a person can let us use that connection.",

      ],

      ],

        "Now move the requirement: A current pass is required for entry. The pass comes before required, but its role hasn't changed. Automatically taking the words after the indicator would point you toward entry and reverse the rule.",
      ],
      prompt: 'How would you diagram: A current pass is required for entry?',

        "Having the pass still doesn't guarantee entry. Someone could keep one in a drawer and never enter. Required means needed for the other condition, not enough to establish that it happened.",
      ],

      ],

function IndicatorSections({ id }: { id: string }) {
  return <>{indicatorExplanations[id].map((lesson, index) => {
    const item = examples[id][index];
    return <Section key={item.word} title={lesson.title} expressionNumber={index + 1}>
      <blockquote>{item.sentence}</blockquote>
      {lesson.paragraphs.map(paragraph => <p key={paragraph}>{paragraph}</p>)}
      <ThinkPause prompt={lesson.prompt}>
        {lesson.reasoning.map(paragraph => <p key={paragraph}>{paragraph}</p>)}
        <Arrow left={item.left} right={item.right}/>
        <p className="co-readback">{item.readback}</p>
      </ThinkPause>
      {lesson.after?.map(paragraph => <p key={paragraph}>{paragraph}</p>)}
      {id === 'group-2' && item.word === 'only if' && <DirectionSwitch/>}
    </Section>;
  })}</>;
}

function Fundamentals({ roles = false }: { roles?: boolean }) {
  return <>
    {!roles && <>
      <Section title="One condition tells you something else">
        <p>A <strong>condition</strong> is something that can be true or false of the situation we're considering. A door is open. A person has a ticket. An order has been packed. Each gives us an idea whose truth we can ask about.</p>
        <p>A <strong>conditional statement</strong> connects two conditions. It tells us that if one is true, the other has to be true too. It doesn't tell us that the first condition actually occurred. It tells us what would follow if it did.</p>
        <p>That distinction matters. You can understand a rule about people who have tickets without knowing whether anyone has a ticket. Later, a fact about one person may give you a way to use the rule.</p>
        <div className="co-intro-relationship"><div><span>One condition is met</span><strong>If this is true...</strong></div><div><span>The statement guarantees another</span><strong>...this has to be true too.</strong></div></div>
        <p>You don't need symbols yet. First, understand what the sentence is saying.</p>
      </Section>
      <Section title="Why learn this?" dark>
        <p>On the LSAT, you're often deciding whether a conclusion follows from what you've been told. A conditional may supply the connection you need. It can also show you exactly where an argument asks you to accept more than its information supports.</p>
        <p>The important part is the direction. If one condition guarantees another, can we start with the other condition and go back? Another statement might allow that. But the first rule alone may not.</p>
        <p>We'll work with one everyday rule and change what we know about a particular order. You'll see a conclusion the rule supports and another that would need more information. That distinction helps you check what must be true and decide whether an argument has gone too far.</p>
      </Section>
      <Section title="A guarantee is stronger than a tendency">
        <p>Compare these two statements:</p>
        <div className="co-intro-relationship"><div><span>A tendency</span><strong>Orders marked ready are usually packed.</strong><p>A ready order could be an exception.</p></div><div><span>A conditional rule</span><strong>Every order marked ready has been packed.</strong><p>A ready order cannot be an exception under this rule.</p></div></div>
        <p>Usually leaves room for exceptions. You could find an order marked ready that hasn't been packed and still accept the first statement. The second doesn't leave that possibility open. Every order with that label has been packed.</p>
        <p>For an LSAT question, take the stated rule as given. A real shop could make a mistake, but we're asking what follows from this particular statement. The rule gives us a guarantee within the information we're considering.</p>
      </Section>
      <Section title="Read one rule in ordinary English">
        <blockquote>Every order marked ready has been packed.</blockquote>
        <p>There are two complete ideas here: an order is <strong>marked ready</strong>, and an order <strong>has been packed</strong>. The sentence tells us something about every order that meets the first condition.</p>
        <p>Read it this way: <strong>if an order is marked ready, then it has been packed.</strong> We don't need to know why the shop uses that label. We need to know what the sentence tells us about an order that has it.</p>
        <p>The rule itself doesn't identify a particular ready order. A separate fact can tell us whether one of the conditions is met in a particular case.</p>
        <ThinkPause prompt="Order A is marked ready. What do we now know about it?">
          <p><strong>Order A has been packed.</strong> The rule covers every order marked ready, and the fact tells us that Order A is one of those orders. That's the connection. The rule tells us what has to be true of the group; the fact lets us apply it to this case.</p>
          <p>We haven't learned that every order in the shop is packed. Our conclusion concerns Order A because that's the order the fact tells us about.</p>
        </ThinkPause>
      </Section>
      <Section title="The arrow is a shorter way to write it">
        <p>Now that we understand the sentence, we can give the two conditions shorter labels. The arrow records the connection between them.</p>
        <Arrow left="Marked ready" right="Packed"/>
        <p>Read it from left to right: <strong>if the order is marked ready, then it has been packed.</strong> The condition on the left gives us enough information to establish the condition on the right under this rule.</p>
        <p>The arrow doesn't mean “and then.” Packing could happen before the label is added. It also doesn't claim the label causes the packing. We're recording what follows logically, not a timeline.</p>
      </Section>
      <Section title="Change the fact, keep the rule">
        <p>Keep the rule exactly the same. This time, the fact tells us about packing instead of the ready label.</p>
        <blockquote>Every order marked ready has been packed.</blockquote>
        <ThinkPause prompt="Order B has been packed. Do we know whether it is marked ready?">
          <p><strong>We don't know yet.</strong> Order B could be marked ready. It could also be packed and waiting for a ready label. Both possibilities fit the statement.</p>
          <p>The rule tells us about every ready order. It hasn't told us that every packed order gets that label. To conclude that Order B is ready, we'd need that additional connection.</p>
        </ThinkPause>
        <p>In the drawing below, ready orders sit inside packed orders because every ready order is packed. A packed order can fit inside or outside the ready group. Use the two facts to compare what each one establishes.</p>
        <SetExplorer/>
      </Section>
      <Section title="Try the same reasoning with a new rule">
        <p>You've used the rule in its stated direction and checked what happens when you start from its result. Try that distinction with a different sentence.</p>
        <Check prompt="Every volunteer wears a badge. Ari wears a badge. Is Ari necessarily a volunteer?" options={['Yes, the badge proves it.', 'No, Ari could have a badge for another reason.']} correct={1} feedback={['You used the rule backward. Every volunteer has a badge, but the sentence does not say everyone with a badge is a volunteer. A staff member wearing one would fit the rule too.', 'A badge alone leaves volunteer status unknown. The sentence allows a staff member with a badge; it has not restricted badges to volunteers.']}/>
        <p>A matching result can make the reverse feel plausible. Check whether the sentence actually gave you that direction before accepting it.</p>
        <p>We can now name the two jobs the conditions are doing. One is enough to establish the other. The other is required whenever the first holds.</p>
      </Section>
    </>}
    {roles && <>
      <Section title="Sufficient means enough">
        <p>An order being marked ready is sufficient for it being packed. It's enough. Once we know the order is marked ready, this rule gives us what we need to conclude it has been packed.</p>
        <blockquote>Every order marked ready has been packed.</blockquote>
        <p>You don't need a second fact about its contents. The rule already tells you what must be true of every order with that label. We call being marked ready the <strong>sufficient condition</strong>. Here, sufficient means enough to establish packing under this particular rule.</p>
        <ThinkPause prompt="Order C is marked ready. Do you need another fact about C to know it has been packed?">
          <p>No. The ready label meets the condition the rule tells us about. The rule and that fact are enough to establish packing.</p>
          <p>This doesn't make the label the only possible way to find out that an order is packed. It is one condition that is enough under this rule.</p>
        </ThinkPause>
        <GateExplorer/>
      </Section>
      <Section title="Enough does not mean the only way">
        <p>Suppose Order D isn't marked ready. We no longer have the fact that allowed us to use the rule in its stated direction. But that doesn't settle the packing question.</p>
        <ThinkPause prompt="Order D isn't marked ready. Could it still have been packed?">
          <p>Yes. D could be packed and waiting for its label. It could also be unpacked. Neither possibility creates a ready order that hasn't been packed, so both fit the rule.</p>
          <p>The sentence gives us one condition that settles packing. It hasn't said packing happens only for those orders. When that sufficient condition isn't present, the other condition may still be true.</p>
        </ThinkPause>
        <p>Use a new rule to check whether you can recognize what is enough.</p>
        <Check prompt="Every delivery marked collected has a pickup receipt. What is sufficient under this rule?" options={['Marked collected', 'Has a pickup receipt']} correct={0} feedback={['Marked collected is enough to establish a pickup receipt. The rule tells us what is true of every delivery with that label.', 'You chose the required result. Having a receipt is not stated enough for the collected label. The sentence gives us the direction from marked collected to receipt, not its reverse.']}/>
      </Section>
      <Section title="Necessary means required">
        <p>Now look at the other condition in the same rule. An order marked ready has to have been packed. Being packed is necessary for being marked ready under this rule.</p>
        <p>We call being packed the <strong>necessary condition</strong>. Necessary means required. It names something that has to be true whenever the sufficient condition is true.</p>
        <p>Ask “required for what?” Here, required for an order marked ready under this rule. The relationship gives the word its meaning.</p>
        <ThinkPause prompt="Which condition does a ready order have to meet under this rule?">
          <p>It has to be packed. Otherwise we'd have a ready order that wasn't packed, which the sentence rules out.</p>
          <p>The ready label is enough to establish packing, and packing is required for every ready order. Those are two views of the same relationship.</p>
        </ThinkPause>
        <div className="co-role-pair"><div><h3>Sufficient</h3><p>Marked ready: enough to establish packing.</p><strong>Goes left</strong></div><div><h3>Necessary</h3><p>Packed: required for every ready order.</p><strong>Goes right</strong></div></div>
      </Section>
      <Section title="Having a requirement does not guarantee the result">
        <p>Let's use a different requirement.</p>
        <blockquote>Entering the archive requires a pass.</blockquote>
        <p>The sentence tells us what someone needs for entry: a pass. If someone enters the archive, they have that pass. That's why has a pass belongs on the required side.</p>
        <Arrow left="Enters the archive" right="Has a pass"/>
        <ThinkPause prompt="Mina has a pass. Does this sentence establish that she entered the archive?">
          <p>No. Mina could have a pass and remain outside. The rule tells us what entry requires; it doesn't tell us that every person with a pass enters.</p>
          <p>Necessary doesn't mean enough. A requirement can be present while the other condition remains unknown. To conclude Mina entered, we'd need information establishing that additional connection.</p>
        </ThinkPause>
        <Check prompt="Every finalist receives an invitation. What is necessary for being a finalist under this rule?" options={['Receiving an invitation', 'Being the winner']} correct={0} feedback={['The rule requires an invitation for each finalist. That makes receiving one necessary for being a finalist under this sentence.', 'You added a condition the sentence has not given us. It says every finalist receives an invitation, not that every finalist wins. The invitation is the requirement stated here.']}/>
      </Section>
      <Section title="Read the roles in the relationship">
        <p>In <strong>Marked ready → Packed</strong>, the left condition is sufficient for the right: it's enough to establish it. The right condition is necessary for the left: it's required whenever the left holds.</p>
        <p>These names describe roles in this rule. A different sentence could give the same idea a different role. Don't ask whether a pass is sufficient or necessary by itself. Ask what the complete sentence says having the pass does.</p>
        <p>The next two groups give us ways to recognize these roles in varied wording. We'll keep returning to the meaning because an indicator can only help if you know what complete idea it refers to.</p>
      </Section>
    </>}
  </>;
}

function GroupLessons({ id }: { id: string }) {
  const group = GROUPS.find(item => item.id === (id === 'group-1' ? 'g1' : 'g2'))!;
  const first = id === 'group-1';
  return <>
    <Section title={first ? 'Find the sufficient idea' : 'Find what is required'}>
      <p>{first
        ? "You already know what a sufficient condition does. When it holds, the rule gives you the other condition. Group 1 helps you recognize that job in several kinds of sentence. We'll work through the meaning of each expression, then practice finding its complete target."
        : "Group 1 helped us find a condition that is enough. Group 2 turns our attention to what must be true when the other condition holds. A requirement belongs on the right because the left condition cannot hold under the rule without it. Having the requirement, though, may leave the left condition unknown."}</p>
      <div className="co-vocabulary">{group.words.map(word => <span key={word}>{word}</span>)}</div>
      <p>An <strong>indicator</strong> is an expression that helps us recognize the relationship. Its <strong>target</strong> is the complete idea it refers to. Finding that idea matters more than taking the next few words in the sentence.</p>
    </Section>
    <IndicatorSections id={id}/>
    <Section title={first ? 'Find the target, then place it' : 'Find the requirement, then place it'}>
      <p>{first
        ? "Add what to the indicator when that gives you a sensible question. If what? All what? The only what? Your answer should be the whole idea the expression refers to. Then check whether that idea really is enough to establish the other condition."
        : "Ask what the indicator refers to. Only what? Only if what? What is required? The target can come before or after the expression, so check its meaning in the complete sentence."}</p>
      <p>Work through the expressions below. First choose the complete target. Then place it on its side of the arrow and read the relationship in ordinary English.</p>
      <TranslationLab id={id}/>
    </Section>
    <Section title="Keep the whole condition" dark>
      <blockquote>{first ? 'Any applicant who submits late pays a fee.' : 'Entry requires a current pass.'}</blockquote>
      <p>{first
        ? "Applicant alone isn't the condition. The sentence is about an applicant who submits late. Keep that restriction when you shorten the idea; otherwise your diagram would make a claim about on-time applicants too."
        : "A current pass is required. Has a pass drops current and would include an expired pass. Shortening a label should save writing while preserving what the sentence requires."}</p>
      <Check prompt={first ? 'What goes left in this rule?' : 'What goes right in this rule?'} options={first ? ['Applicant', 'Applicant submits late'] : ['Has current pass', 'Has any pass']} correct={first ? 1 : 0} feedback={first
        ? ['You dropped the late-submission restriction. Applicant alone would cover every applicant, including someone who submits on time. The sufficient idea is applicant submits late.', 'This keeps the complete sufficient idea. The rule covers applicants who submit late, so keep that restriction with the applicant.']
        : ['This keeps the full requirement. Entry needs a current pass under the rule; an expired pass does not meet it.', 'You dropped current from the requirement. Has any pass would include an expired pass, which is not what the sentence requires.']}/>
    </Section>
    <Section title={first ? 'Read the only as a complete expression' : 'Compare only with the only'}>
      {first ? <>
        <blockquote>The only people admitted are members.</blockquote>
        <p>The only what? The only people admitted. The complete target is admitted people. If someone is admitted, the sentence tells us they're a member.</p>
        <Arrow left="Admitted" right="Member"/>
        <p>A member who stays outside fits this rule. Membership hasn't been made enough for admission. Check that your diagram keeps that possibility open.</p>
        <Check prompt="The only vehicles permitted inside are electric. Which diagram preserves the rule?" options={['Electric → Permitted inside', 'Permitted inside → Electric']} correct={1} feedback={['You made electric status enough for permission. The sentence requires permitted vehicles to be electric; it does not promise admission to every electric vehicle.', 'Permitted vehicles have to be electric. This direction preserves the limit on permitted vehicles without adding a promise about all electric vehicles.']}/>
      </> : <>
        <div className="co-word-comparison"><div><blockquote>Only members are admitted.</blockquote><p>Only refers to members. Membership is required for admission, so member goes right.</p></div><div><blockquote>The only people admitted are members.</blockquote><p>The only refers to admitted people. Admission is enough to establish membership, so admitted goes left.</p></div></div>
        <Arrow left="Admitted" right="Member"/>
        <p>Both sentences express this relationship. The expressions help us locate different targets, but the complete meaning determines the same direction.</p>
        <Check prompt="Only registered guests receive wristbands. What follows from receiving a wristband?" options={['The person is a registered guest.', 'Nothing about registration.']} correct={0} feedback={['Only limits wristbands to registered guests. Receiving a wristband therefore establishes registration under this rule.', 'You treated the sentence like all registered guests receive wristbands. Only restricts who receives one, so the wristband does establish that the person is a registered guest.']}/>
      </>}
    </Section>
    <Section title="From sentence to diagram">
      <p>You have seen the expressions with help. Now use a new sentence. Identify both complete ideas, choose the sufficient one for the left, and check whether your diagram says what the sentence says.</p>
      <p>If you know the meaning but hesitate over the arrow, imagine the left condition is true. Does the sentence then require the right condition? Read the whole relationship in English. If it makes a promise the original didn't make, change the direction.</p>
      <DiagramBuilder id={id}/>
      <details className="co-practical-note"><summary>Why write a diagram when I understand the sentence?</summary><p>For one short sentence, you may be able to hold the connection in your head. Here, writing it makes your direction and complete conditions visible so you can check them. If your first diagram doesn't match the meaning, find the exact phrase you misread and revise that part.</p></details>
    </Section>
    <Section title="Say the rule without the scaffold">
      <p>Read the new sentence and explain its direction before revealing. If you hesitate, ask what the indicator refers to, then try the proposed relationship in ordinary English. Compare your explanation with the one that appears.</p>
      <Flashcards id={id}/>
    </Section>
    <Section title="Check the meaning, not just the word">
      <Check prompt={first ? 'A report is reviewed if submitted before noon. Which is the same rule?' : 'A student graduates only if the project is completed. Which is the same rule?'} options={first ? ['If reviewed, it was submitted before noon.', 'If submitted before noon, it is reviewed.'] : ['If the student graduates, the project was completed.', 'If the project is completed, the student graduates.']} correct={first ? 1 : 0} feedback={first
        ? ['You reversed the if relationship. Submission before noon is enough for review; the sentence has not said review proves when the report was submitted.', 'This preserves the if-clause as the sufficient condition. Submission before noon gives us review even though it appears second in the original sentence.']
        : ['This preserves project completion as a requirement for graduation. It does not turn completing the project into a promise of graduation.', 'You turned the only-if requirement into a guarantee. Graduation requires completion, but completion alone is not stated enough to graduate.']}/>
      <p>The guided practice asks you to write your reasoning with the method beside you. Then the attached drill gives you fresh questions. Use the explanation to inspect the direction and complete conditions, not only whether you chose the same answer.</p>
    </Section>
  </>;
}

export function ConditionalOpeningLesson({ unit, onComplete, continueHref, continueLabel = 'Continue to guided practice', previousHref, reviewed }: ConditionalLessonNoteProps) {
  const [motionPaused, setMotionPaused] = useState(false);
  const group = unit.id === 'group-1' || unit.id === 'group-2';
  const orientation = unit.id === 'orientation';
  const title = group ? unit.id === 'group-1' ? 'Group 1: what is enough?' : 'Group 2: what is required?' : orientation ? 'What are conditionals?' : 'What is enough, and what is required?';
  const subtitle = orientation
    ? "A conditional tells us that if one thing is true, something else has to be true too. Let's see what that connection lets you conclude, and what it leaves open."
    : group ? unit.id === 'group-1'
      ? 'These expressions can point to the sufficient idea. Read what each one says before deciding which complete condition belongs on the left.'
      : 'These expressions can identify a requirement. Find the complete idea the sentence says you need, then check what its presence does and does not prove.'
    : "The same rule gives its two conditions different jobs. Let's take each one seriously before giving it a place in the diagram.";
  return <div className="conditional-note co-opening" data-motion-paused={motionPaused}>
    <DynamicIslandTOC key={unit.id} selector=".co-opening [data-toc]"/>
    <header className={'co-hero ' + (orientation ? 'co-intro-hero' : '')}>
      <p className="co-kicker">Conditional logic</p><h1>{title}</h1><p>{subtitle}</p>
      <a href="#co-reading">{orientation ? 'Start with the meaning' : 'Begin reading'} <span aria-hidden="true">↓</span></a>
      <button type="button" className="co-motion-toggle" aria-pressed={motionPaused} onClick={() => setMotionPaused(!motionPaused)}>{motionPaused ? 'Resume motion' : 'Pause motion'}</button>
      {!orientation && <div className="co-hero-orbit" aria-hidden="true"><span>Enough</span><i>→</i><span>Required</span></div>}
    </header>
    <article id="co-reading">
      {group ? <GroupLessons id={unit.id}/> : <Fundamentals roles={unit.id === 'sufficient-necessary'}/>}
      <ConditionalOpeningMedia unitId={unit.id}/>
      <footer className="co-footer">
        <p>{reviewed ? 'You marked this lesson as read. You can return to the examples whenever you need.' : 'Marking this lesson as read records review. Your practice gives you a chance to use the reasoning yourself.'}</p>
        <div className="co-choices">{previousHref && <Link to={previousHref}>Previous lesson</Link>}<button type="button" onClick={onComplete}>{reviewed ? 'Lesson read' : 'Mark lesson as read'}</button><Link className="co-primary" to={continueHref}>{continueLabel} <span aria-hidden="true">→</span></Link></div>
      </footer>
    </article>
  </div>;
}
`;

text(await tools.apply_patch(patch));
